Who says a state on the West Coast wants low/unskilled labor.  

Before computers were being built in that state, plenty of clothing was designed and built there (denim is still heavily produced in that region). This manufacturing long left the state in the late 80s/early 90s and there likely won't be any push to get most of that back. The only major "plant" I'm aware of in that state is the one operated by a well-known electric vehicle manufacturer, and I'm sure every representative from that state will sign a blank check to the CEO to keep most of it there.

This state has a very unique situation where it can attract all levels of skill. Between its colleges and its companies, there is a heavy demand for highly skilled labor to design "things" -- there simply isn't a huge demand to build those "things". So many other countries have already mastered the art of building, why does this state need it back?

The big companies that have left this state include major automotive manufacturers: one from Japan and another from the same country. The first left for a southern state -- not only for the low taxes, but because the manufacturing plants were already in that state (moving to that location also cut hundreds to thousands of jobs). The second is moving their main headquarters to another southern state, but none of their research and development. They will also likely lose ~30-50% of their workforce by moving (contractors to full-time employees is nearly 2:1, they won't move any contractors). Between the tax savings of simply getting out of that state, the tax breaks that the new state will provide, and the sheer number of people that won't relocate (several of my neighbors work at that company, they aren't going), you're looking at massive savings by simply changing their point of operation.

What I'm trying to say is: looking strictly at companies leaving this state for another southern state is a misnomer. You need to dig into the details as to why these companies are leaving and understand that it's not JUST lower wages and tax breaks.

Of course it does, indirectly, that all trickles down.

This has been an economic plan since the 80s and it has been proven that it doesn't work.

You start taking large numbers of incomes out of a populous state and you'll start seeing demand falling across the various markets, lessening the various resource demands, including unskilled labor.

You're actually listing something that residents of that state *should* want: get more people to leave the area. People leaving from the congested urban centers would increase the number of available houses. With a surplus of housing, rents would have to be decreased to keep them filled. The cost of living in those urban areas is very high, with no plans to build vertically and a lack of affordable housing. Getting enough people to move out of those cities would help reduce the costs for everyone in the region.

The numbers of jobs and people leaving from that state are in the four and maybe five figure range. The state has a population of ~18 million people and it would have to take *many* more people to leave before any changes were made for business taxes or incentives. Giving companies a tax break once will make them threaten to do it again -- you have to accept that if they want to move, they *will* move.

Demand does it all -- it's Econ 101.

Increasing the minimum will put more money into the pockets of people. More money in their pockets (that isn't offset with higher expenses) will give them more money to spend.

Shouldn't the average wage be higher than the current minimum if the demand were already there? If not, I would think that raising it would only lessen demand and create a surplus of workers.

The average wage *is* higher than the minimum; it's part of the definition differences between minimum and average. You're looking at the raise in minimum wage purely from a business perspective.

Think about the situation if you're in the shoes of someone making the minimum -- you have MORE to spend. YOU create a higher demand, NOT the business. Now that YOU are demanding more of something, businesses will try to cater to your demands. If one business can't handle the demand, more will follow.

Let's also remember that the minimum wage is for a specific city and for businesses with 25 or more employees. If you opened a taco restaurant (we can always use more) and are employing 25 people, your business sounds like it's healthy and thriving. Small businesses that have fewer than 25 employees should be welcoming this sort of increase, as now they can have new customers available because there will be more demand.

But I thought an increased number of businesses is what creates the demand, then in turn pulling up the wage.

The opposite is actually true. Businesses satisfy a demand. If there are lots of businesses in the area, what's stopping them from lowering the wages? You increase wages because you have to hire people to supply demand. If you're oversaturated in the ability to supply the demand, you don't need to pay high wages anymore and can easily let people go.

If you want to push your analogy in the other direction: why not open a high-end wedding cake shop in the middle of the lowest income area? You've now created a business that can pay good wages (as your prices are high), but there isn't any demand in the area for your cakes with the high cost. It would make no economic sense for this, but that's where your analogy can go.

As a user and owner of these devices, I can emphatically say that this will NOT be the future for all fighting games (let alone the specific series).

These are things that are much easier for me to do on this type of controller:

- Instant air moves. Specifically, moves that don't have a height requirement.

- Comboing into a specific character's ultimate move. Just spam the buttons and you're good to go.

- Charge motions.

- Quarter-circle forward/quarter-circle back and dashing feel "faster". Your mileage may vary.

- Focus Attack Dash Cancel moves *are* faster, but I haven't quite mastered the timing for it.

- Full rotation motions are great! It's a three-button press: forward, back, down + up + attack. Once you learn the timing on this, it feels sneaky.

Things that are not so good:

- Tiring. After an hour or so, my left hand is definitely tired. I've played many hours at a time, but I'm simply not as comfortable with it compared to a traditional arcade stick. Potentially a "left-handed" version would play better for me, not sure.

- Special move motions don't feel as fast. You can go forward, down, forward + punch on this controller, but it feels slower than a stick with the "wiggle" motion. The shortcut can be helpful, but it's also tiring to hold down a button and then double tap.

- Full rotation motions are 100% difficult. Yes, I've watched the tutorial. Yes, I've put practice into this motion. I simply can't.

- "Zig zag" motions (specific character moves) are a little more difficult than a stick. While I can do them on both sides, I definitely prefer it on a stick.

There are a few characters I feel GREAT with playing and a few that I 100% avoid (typically grapplers that need/have a full rotation motion). Then there are characters I like to play, but are simply tiring to use (divekick and charge characters, specifically).

In addition to what I posted above, the game engine doesn't handle this type of controller all too well:

- There is a lot of height restriction on moves, so you're not going to instant air everything. A specific character's move is a terrible option, but the instant air makes it viable -- shame it has a height restriction.

- Leniency on inputs can still cause moves you don't want to come out.

While I *like* the controller, there are definitely trade-offs. Some have adapted very well to using one, and I've given nearly 2+ years of using it on a weekly basis to understand my own limitations.

Comparing the installation process of a popular operating system to that of a widely used open-source alternative reveals a stark contrast in design objectives.

> Locked to a tiny resolution

Given the vast array of graphic cards available globally, selecting a low resolution for the installation process isn't particularly problematic. The primary aim of the operating system is to swiftly transition users to the desktop, and having a native resolution during installation doesn't provide significant advantages.

> Bundles absolutely no software but the install script itself

What do you mean by this? Operating systems are responsible for managing various components such as user interfaces, network configurations, and storage systems. The popular operating system installs several useful applications, including a web browser (which is essential for downloading other software), a basic text editor, and command line tools. In contrast, many open-source installers I encounter include minimal software at boot (like certain server distributions) and require additional downloads after the operating system is up and running.

> Lacks drivers upon the first boot

Which drivers are you referring to? Are you talking about high-end RAID controllers, graphics, audio, or network drivers? I can provide numerous examples where a standard installation of a certain open-source operating system fails to recognize specific hardware components.

Most users simply want the installation to detect the network card so they can complete the setup process.

> Awful partition utility (although you can get by with shift+F10 and diskpart)

The installer for the more recent versions of the popular operating system allows users to create multiple partitions on individual drives without needing to resort to command line tools. What specific partitioning requirements do you have that cannot be addressed through the graphical interface of this operating system?

Keep in mind: the goal of this operating system is to install itself on your drive and serve as your primary OS. If your requirements extend beyond this, you need to plan accordingly.

> Buggy as hell! The latest version has failed to install on any machine with at least one SSD and one HDD I've tried. It also randomly fails if you plug it into a USB 3 slot.

Out of the millions of installations of this operating system, the number of failures is not nearly as high as you suggest. This operating system does not install onto USB drives; it only recognizes drives that do not appear removable (a design choice that has persisted since earlier versions). Installing it onto a bootable drive is possible but requires considerable effort, and this is well documented.

The open-source alternative is designed to accommodate a wide range of needs and roles, which is why its installation process is significantly more adaptable. The popular operating system is intended to be your primary OS and will function smoothly... when conditions allow.

Not a problem.

A popular operating system uses the VESA standards for its graphical installers. It started with a resolution of 640x480, moved up to 800x600, and finally improved to 1024x768. Why bother trying to achieve native resolution when the installer works with keyboard shortcuts?

I am talking about the software bundled with the installation media. Essentially, more than just the install script itself.

The installer is fully scriptable to the point where you can input the install key, activate, and install other software.

Or provide yourself with the appropriate tools. You assume I have intrinsic knowledge of the machine I'm about to install the operating system on.

The only thing the operating system wants to do is install to your drive, period. All other considerations beyond where to install are not important and can be handled after the reboots.

Because the overwhelming majority of those are installed by manufacturers onto standardized hardware. Trust me, they have much better tools to work with than just a USB drive, and they absolutely do not run the installer in the typical manner.

As I mentioned earlier, the installer can be fully customizable. Take your install ISO, extract the files, and rebuild your own ISO to fit your needs. Corporations have specific needs, manufacturers have completely different needs, and it sounds like you have your own requirements.

99.999% of end users do not have the same needs.

Also, "works on my machine" is never a pertinent argument to make.

How many machines have you installed this operating system on? I've done it on a few hundred (volunteering at a local school district), and all of them were able to install the operating system without any issues. The only machines that had problems (most were donated) with the installer were those with RAID cards (requiring drivers) or EFI-related BIOS settings (needing to switch to legacy boot).

The install decisions were built around one thing: install as soon as possible, so the user can use the graphical interface to complete the rest. Because of this design decision, the only real limitation for the installer is finding valid, non-removable disks. Previous installers handled various tasks with video, audio, and networking—all of which have been dropped to focus on the essential task of finding local disks.

I get a weird vibe from these posts. Some kind of "I don't personally need X so I don't see why anybody else would" mentality.

Please understand that I've been installing operating systems on machines since the mid-90s. My installation experience has been via scripted corporate installs, netboot, floppy disks, DVDs, and USB sticks. For the longest period of time, the installer has had one goal in mind: get the operating system onto your machine with as few clicks as necessary.

A web browser. A file manager. A hardware monitor. Just about any damn thing you can think of.

These are nice to haves, but not important for an install (in my humble opinion). All I want for the operating system is to find the disk, update the master boot record, and start the multitude of reboots to complete the setup.

Why not provide a graphical user interface to complete the rest as soon as possible? This is Mr. and Mrs. Everybody we're talking about.

The operating system *is* providing you a GUI as soon as possible: you just need to reboot to do it. I get it, you want installers to be more like those from Linux distributions that are GUI based. *I* want the operating system install to have even fewer clicks/key presses to install -- just get me to the disk selection and hurry up for the GUI.

Did you know that one of the oldest Unix-like installs didn't even prompt? You put in the CD/DVD and it takes the first disk, partitions, and begins the install. If you had some data or an OS on that first drive, it was a goner.

Let's not for a split second delude ourselves into believing the installer is anything more than mediocre and barely sufficient.

The installer is mediocre, but it was never meant to be a power user's tool. All the company wants to do with the installer is find your disk, install the operating system, and get you to a GUI to complete the rest. With that design goal in mind, it's perfectly fine.

So now artists get to happily go back to being paid next to nothing for their work.

What do *you* define as proper compensation for an artist's work? The recording industry and labels have their own definition, to which plenty of artists have agreed to those terms.

Every song out there has a myriad of pieces that need to get paid:

1. Studio time.
2. Producers.
3. Mixers.
4. Writers.
5. Performers (album and live are different, but we'll treat them the same in this argument).

Independent artists have little funds to rent studio time, hire producers, mixers and may be the only one performing the music for any given track or album -- this is why they seek representation from labels for their work. Once they have representation, they can ask for loans to hire out the necessary people to finish their recordings.

Given all the people I listed, how much should a well-known pop artist be making on their most recent single? Clearly, they're performing on that track, check. Did they write it? Did they produce (fund) it? Did they record it in their own studio? Did they mix it? How about the other musicians that played on that track ... where is their compensation? If I'm looking at this correctly, that artist may "only" be 1/5th of the team it took to get that ONE single out to the masses.

Before we even try to calculate how much their one performance is worth, let's also forget the major factor in the room: marketing. That artist's face, name and voice are all over the place! Imagine if they weren't a household name and still had this single -- it likely wouldn't be nearly as popular.

Artists have a choice with their work. Sign and they gain access to funds, marketing and a slew of resources to help bring their work to the masses. Not sign and it will be entirely up to them (financially) to get their work out to the masses. But I do wish that the professional football league didn't claim to be a non-profit business!

The league is a non-profit business for the following reasons:

1. The league is funded via post-tax dollars that the owners collect from advertising revenue, stadium revenue, licensing agreements, etc.

2. Every team is taxed, every stadium is taxed, every player is taxed. How much they are taxed (each) is all about how good their accountants set them up to be. Make no mistake, everyone is getting their share (owners, players, tax authorities, etc).

3. Each team is an individual corporation, owned by people that have different voting rights, etc. Because each corporation wants their revenue to grow, they have given up some individual rights to the league (run by the commissioner) in order to help grow it for everyone.

Every professional sports league is set up in the same way: every team is responsible to pay the players, every player is responsible for their taxes and a portion of post-tax dollars goes to run the league itself -- for the better of everyone. The actual league offices are in major cities, where they likely employ fewer people than what it takes to run a stadium (and team). Any money generated by the league itself (NOT any individual team) is VERY small -- show me someone that actually bought a non-team specific hat/shirt/jersey.

If salary caps were removed completely, then large market teams (like those in major metropolitan areas) would absolutely dominate smaller market teams in their ability to spend. Even if maximum contracts remain in place (I'm not convinced it will lead to significant changes), it still won't benefit players with free agency options who want to leave.
